extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying U.S. patent remedies and doctrines (late 19th-century cases)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts doctrinal rules and standards from a legal treatise appendix regarding patent damages, proofs, re-issue practice, reduction to practice, term/foreign-patent effects, marking, and related procedural matters in U.S. case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full-profits recovery requires whole market value due to invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff cannot recover the entire profits unless the whole market value were due to his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patented feature is not the sole reason for the article's market value, full profits are not recoverable. (See Fay v. Allen (1887).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of entire profits when defendant's entire profit derived from plaintiff's invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the entire profit of the defendant is derived from the plaintiff's invention, the plaintiff is entitled to recover it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the infringing product's profits are wholly traceable to the patented invention, full disgorgement is available. (See Hurlburt v. Schillinger (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire profit recovery when patented feature gives entire efficiency/salability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the entire efficiency and salability of an invention depend on the patented feature the patentee is entitled to recover all the profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patented element is what makes the product valuable, the patentee may claim all defendant profits. (See McDonald v. Whitney (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on defendant to apportion profits for own improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the defendant's burden to show what part of his profits was due to his own improvements when the plaintiff's invention apparently gave the device its market value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plaintiff's invention produced the market value, defendant must prove the share attributable to non-infringing features. (See Morss v. Union Form Co. (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits measured by advantage over available non-patented methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits are the advantage derived by the infringer over what he would have obtained by adopting some other available method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare defendant's gains from the infringing device to the gains obtainable using prior or public-domain means. (See Shannon v. Brunner (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare infringing device to previously employed devices
rubrics_metrics.description: In estimating profits the advantage of using the infringing device is to be compared with that of using devices previously employed for the same purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prior art or prior commercial devices as the baseline for measuring advantage. (See Coupe v. Weatherhead (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits are what defendant made or saved versus free-public means
rubrics_metrics.description: The profits of the defendant are what he made or saved over what could have been saved or made by using means free to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify gains relative to freely available alternatives. (See McMuny v. Emerson (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits measured as advantage over equally adequate public means
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits are to be measured by the advantage received by the defendant over what he would have enjoyed by using other means then open to the public and adequate to obtain an equally beneficial result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only advantages attributable to the patented novelty, not to public-domain substitutes, are recoverable. (See Webster Loom Co. v. Higgins (1889); Tilghman v. Proctor (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit measure may be price differential when using patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant's profit may be measured by the amount charged by him when using the patented invention in excess of that charged when he does not use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare defendant's pricing/receipts in periods/products with and without the patented feature. (See Vulcanite Paving Co. v. American Artificial Stone Pavement Co. (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits from use of patented composition giving device value
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patented composition used in making a device gives it its value, the patentee is entitled to the entire profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the composition is the value-creating component, full disgorgement applies. (See Welling v. La Bau (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-profits measured by difference with/without design
rubrics_metrics.description: The profits on a design are the difference between the profits of articles with it and without it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate incremental profit attributable solely to the design. (See Tomkinson v. Willets Mfg. Co. (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest on profits generally disallowed before master's report date
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally interest is not to be allowed on profits before the date of the submission of the master's report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-report interest is typically excluded. (See Tilghman v. Proctor (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: If profits cannot be shown, award nominal damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Where on an accounting it does not appear what definite profits were due to the invention, only nominal damages can be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computation is impossible or unsupported, courts award nominal damages rather than speculative sums. (See Roemer v. Simon (1887); Fischer v. Hayes (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages limited to plaintiff's actual deprivation; excess profits not recoverable as damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits made by the defendant, in excess of those of which the plaintiff was deprived, cannot be recovered as damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages compensate plaintiff's loss; disgorgement of excess speculative gains is constrained. (See Morss v. Union Form Co. (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation rules adopted in part of case bind subsequent proceedings in that case
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule for computing profits adopted in one part of a case will be followed in the future proceedings in that case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court-adopted accounting methods in a case are applied for consistency during the same litigation. (See Webster Loom Co. v. Higgins (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing a caveat is not reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a caveat is not reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A caveat filing does not constitute the act of reducing an invention to practice. (See Elges v. Miller (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Working model intended as such is not necessarily reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A working model designed and intended as such is not reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designing/making a model alone may not suffice to prove practical reduction; context matters. (See Green v. Hall (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings filed in Patent Office are not reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are not reduction though filed in the Patent Office, nor do they show a practical embodiment sufficient to save the rights of the first conceiver as against a later rival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper drawings do not substitute for an actual reduction to practice. (See Beach v. Fowler (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office cannot determine reduction-to-practice factually
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office has no means of determining whether or not an invention has been reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice is a factual matter for courts/juries, not simply the Office. (See Green v. Hall (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue can only cover what original intended to embrace
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue can cover only what an examination of the original in the light of the re-issue shows that the original was intended to embrace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue cannot claim matter beyond what the original patent fairly disclosed as intended. (See Flower v. Detroit (1888); Hoskin v. Fisher (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot cover matter not described/claimed after intervening rights arose
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot cover matter which the original did not describe or claim, after intervening rights have arisen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If third-party rights intervened, new subject matter cannot be added by re-issue. (See Dunham v. Dennison Mfg. Co. (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Introducing radically different invention in re-issue after long delay is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction into a re-issue of an invention radically different from the original after long delay is fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant substantive broadening long after issuance undermines re-issue validity. (See Hubel v. Dick (1886).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee cannot re-issue so as to broaden the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee cannot so re-issue as to broaden the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignee's re-issue cannot enlarge coverage beyond original inventor's intent. (See Ex parte Mahnken (1887).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue of combination patent may cover subcombinations/elements within reasonable time
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue of a combination-patent within reasonable time may cover subcombinations and elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited narrowing/adjustment allowed early; timing is critical. (See Hubel v. Dick (1886).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot insert process claim into re-issue of apparatus/product unless single invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for the process cannot be inserted into the re-issue of a patent for the apparatus or product, or vice versa, unless they are so related to each other as to constitute but one invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process, apparatus, and product claims can be mixed only when they form a single inventive concept. (See Ex parte Tainter (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot enlarge claims unless clear inadvertent mistake in wording
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot enlarge Claims unless there has been a clear mistake inadvertently committed in wording them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadening requires proof of inadvertent clerical/wording error, not mere desire to expand scope. (See Huber v. N. O. Nelson Mfg. Co. (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot enlarge a claim by omitting an element previously claimed as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot enlarge a Claim by omitting an element previously claimed as essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing an essential element to broaden scope is impermissible. (See Matthews v. Iron Clad Mfg. Co. (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue with enlarged claims to cover matter in public use after unreasonable delay is void
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue with enlarged Claims to cover matter already in public use after unreasonable delay is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay that allows public adoption bars later expansion via re-issue. (See Flower v. Detroit (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim restricted by Patent Office in first re-issue cannot be enlarged by subsequent re-issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim restricted by direction of the Patent Office in the first re-issue cannot be enlarged by subsequent re-issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office-imposed restrictions on re-issue claims are binding in later re-issues. (See Yale Lock Co. v. James (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue to restore a claim rejected with applicant's acquiescence is invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue to restore a Claim rejected by the Patent Office with the acquiescence of the applicant is invalid though applied for within two years after the original was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquiescence to rejection precludes later restoration via re-issue. (See Union Paper Bag Mach. Co. v. Waterbury (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may correct errors due to mistaken ideas of Patent Office objections
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may correct errors occasioned by mistaken ideas of the objections raised in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors caused by misconceived Office objections can justify limited re-issue corrections. (See Hutchinson v. Everett (1887).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonable delay in applying for re-issue is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays in applying for a re-issue may be fatal to the re-issued patent and may be taken advantage of by a demurrer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is a jurisdictional/practical requirement; excessive unexplained delay undermines re-issue. (See Philadelphia Novelty Mfg. Co. v. Rouss (1889); Hutchinson v. Everett (1887).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner has no jurisdiction over re-issue unless filed within reasonable time
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner has no jurisdiction over an application for re-issue unless it is filed within a reasonable time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictional bar if not timely filed; reasonableness is a legal question for courts. (See Hutchinson v. Everett (1887); Hoskin v. Fisher (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay reasonableness is question of law for courts, Patent Office decision not conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether delay in applying for a re-issue is reasonable is a question of law for the court, and the decision of the Patent Office on that point is not conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts can review the Office's timeliness findings. (See Hoskin v. Fisher (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadvertence/mistake for re-issue must refer to application, not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Inadvertence or mistake must exist in reference to the application, not the invention, and the re-issue must be confined to the invention inadvertently misdescribed or misclaimed in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue justification must be rooted in application-level errors, not attempts to claim new inventive matter. (See Ex parte Mahnken (1887).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee aware of Office-imposed limitations cannot later claim inadvertence
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee taking his patent with full knowledge of the limitations imposed by the Patent Office and the consequent imperfection of his Claims, cannot set up inadvertence, etc., as a ground for a re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual knowledge of limitations negates later assertions of inadvertence. (See Ex parte Page (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence in rejection indicates exclusion not inadvertent
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiescence in the rejection of a Claim by the Patent Office shows that the exclusion of the matter claimed was not inadvertent or accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant's conduct before the Office is evidence against later re-issue claims. (See Union Paper Bag Mach. Co. v. Waterbury (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's decision on inadvertence etc. reviewable by courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision of the Commissioner as to inadvertence, accident, or mistake, may be reviewed by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial review available for Office decisions on re-issue grounds. (See Huber v. N. O. Nelson Mfg. Co. (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's oath to inadvertence is substantive (not perfunctory)
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath of the inventor to his inadvertence, etc., is not perfunctory, though he has assigned his interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor's sworn statements carry weight even after assignment. (See Ex parte Mahnken (1887).)

rubrics_metrics.name: No action on a patent after its surrender pending re-issue application
rubrics_metrics.description: No action can be maintained on a patent after its surrender and pending an application for re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrender suspends enforceability during re-issue processing. (See Burrell v. Hackley (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Original patent admissible evidence on re-issue validity
rubrics_metrics.description: On the question of the validity of a re-issue the original patent is admissible evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original patent may be used to determine whether re-issue matches original invention. (See Oregon Improvement Co. v. Excelsior Coal Co. (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: United States may sue in equity to repeal a patent obtained by fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States may sue in equity for the repeal of a patent obtained by fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government has equitable remedy to nullify fraudulently obtained patents. (See United States v. American Bell Telephone Co. (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking rules: cannot mark whole article patented if parts unpatented
rubrics_metrics.description: An article covering new, valuable, unpatented matter as well as parts that are patented cannot be marked 'patented' as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only patented portions may be indicated; mis-marking may infer deceptive intent. (See DeVerall v. Banker (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and consequence of 'patented' stamp
rubrics_metrics.description: The stamp 'patented' means that the article is protected by a patent at the time of sale, and if the patent has expired the mark is false; intent to deceive will be inferred from the act of marking itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False marking consequences and inference of intent arise from stamping after patent expiration. (See New York Card Co. v. Union Card Co. (1886).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to deceive in marking must be proved
rubrics_metrics.description: In marking 'with intent to deceive' the intent to deceive is essential and must be proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although inference from marking exists, legal proof of intent remains required. (See DeVerall v. Banker (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Patent applied for' marking is not an offense
rubrics_metrics.description: To mark an unpatented article with 'Patent applied for' is not an offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted marking while application is pending. (See Schwebel v. Bothe (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: State control over sale of invention and taxation of proceeds
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of an inventor to sell his invention is not derived from the Patent Law and may be controlled by the State authorities; a State cannot tax the property in letters-patent, but may tax the proceeds thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State statutes may regulate sales; taxation distinguishes patent as property versus proceeds. (See Herdic v. Roessler (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of American patent may be proved by parol
rubrics_metrics.description: The American patent need not declare its true term on its face, but the exact limit may be proved by parol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic/parol evidence admissible to establish patent term. (See Bate Refrigerating Co. v. Hammond (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic patent term can be limited by prior foreign patent
rubrics_metrics.description: An American patent may expire with the prior foreign patent when the American covers some improvements if the invention is substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign patent priority can limit domestic exclusivity when inventions overlap. (See Holmes Electric Protective Co. v. Metropolitan Burglar Alarm Co. (1887); Siemens' Administrator v. Sellers (1887).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic patent expires with foreign even if domestic includes inseparable added features
rubrics_metrics.description: A domestic patent expires with the foreign one, though the former includes other features which are not separable inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-separable additional features do not prevent expiration tied to the foreign patent's term. (See Chirk v. Wilson (1886).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patent first issued limits domestic even if domestic first applied for
rubrics_metrics.description: The domestic patent will be limited by the term of the foreign if the foreign were first issued, though the domestic were first applied for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issue date of foreign patent can govern domestic term. (See Edison Electric Light Co. v. U. S. Electric Lighting Co. (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign antedating (English issued after but antedated) does not limit domestic term
rubrics_metrics.description: When an English patent is issued after the American, but is antedated to precede it, the term of the latter is not limited thereby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antedating does not override actual issuance order for term limitation purposes. (See Seibert Cylinder Oil Co. v. William Powell Co. (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patent limits domestic regardless of who holds foreign patent with consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The foreign patent will limit the term of the domestic whether it were granted to the same patentee or to some other person with his consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent/assignment relationships do not prevent foreign limitation. (See Edison Electric Light Co. v. U. S. Electric Lighting Co. (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of foreign patent may extend domestic when foreign extension is a matter of right
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension of the term of a foreign patent by which that of the American patent is limited does now extend the latter, where the foreign extension is a matter of right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If foreign statute gives an extension as of right, domestic term may follow that extension. (See Bate Refrigerating Co. v. Hammond (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of foreign patent does not necessarily terminate domestic patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of the domestic patent does not expire with the forfeiture of the foreign patent by failure to pay periodical taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forfeiture by foreign patentee for non-payment does not automatically end U.S. patent term (some cases hold otherwise; doctrine evolving). (See Paillard v. Bruno (1886).)

rubrics_metrics.name: American patent granted after foreign patent's forfeiture is of doubtful validity for injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: An American patent granted after the forfeiture of a foreign one for the same invention is of too doubtful validity to warrant an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may decline equitable relief where validity is questionable due to prior foreign forfeiture. (See Huber v. Myers Sanitary Depot (1887).)

rubrics_metrics.name: No injunctive relief for unlawful use before patent issues (even if application pending)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unlawful use of an invention will not be enjoined before a patent has issued, though an application be pending in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pending applications do not confer issuance-based injunctive rights. (See Rein v. Clayton (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor has property in invention pre-issuance until public disclosure; equity protects against unfair piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor has a property in his invention, independent of any patent, until he makes it public, and it will meanwhile be protected against piracy by unfair means by the State courts of equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable principles can protect secret inventions pre-patent if confidentiality/unfairness present. (See Tabor v. Hoffman (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent grants exclusion right only, not affirmative right to make/use/sell
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent grants to the patentee only the right to exclude others from practising the invention, not the right to make, use, or sell it himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee's rights are negative (exclusionary); other laws/regulations may control making/using/selling. (See Herdic v. Roessler (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: No property right in invention until patent issues (contrasting views exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no property right in an invention until the patent issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some authorities hold there is no legal property right pre-issuance; this is context-dependent and contested in cases. (See Marsh v. Nichols (1888).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discoverer of inventor's secret (without breach of trust) may use invention pre-patent without liability
rubrics_metrics.description: One who discovers the inventor's secret by dishonorable means, but without a breach of trust may use the invention before patent without liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable remedies may not bar such use absent breach of fiduciary duty. (See Hortenhaus v. American Watch Co. (1884).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility does not mean commercial success; gambling uses not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility does not mean commercial success; an invention employed only for gambling is not useful or patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court assesses lawful, practical utility, not mere market success; illegal/gambling uses fail utility requirement. (See Anilin v. Levinstein (1887); National Automatic Devices Co. v. Lloyd (1889).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of others' efforts may show utility; a user cannot deny utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The efforts of others to accomplish a result may show that the means by which it is accomplished has utility; one using an invention cannot deny its utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrent independent attempts support utility; accused infringer's use concedes utility. (See Shannon v. Brewer (1887); La Rue v. Western Electric Co. (1887).)
